132 Dīgha Nikāya Sīlakkhandhavagga Sāmaññaphala Sutta

In the same way, Great King, a monk drenches, permeates, fills, and suffuses this very body with a happiness divested of rapture. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with this happiness divested of rapture.

This, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life, visible in this very life, which is more excellent and sublime than the previous fruits of the ascetic life.

68. Furthermore, Great King, with the giving up of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a monk enters and remains in the fourth <term>jhāna</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss>, which is beyond pleasure and pain and possesses purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. He sits suffusing this very body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with a pure, bright mind.

Just as if, Great King, a man were sitting wrapped from head to foot in a white cloth, so that there would be no part of his entire body not covered by that white cloth; even so, Great King, the monk sits suffusing this very body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with a pure, bright mind.

This, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life, visible in this very life, which is more excellent and sublime than the previous fruits of the ascetic life.

69. Furthermore, Great King, when the mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfections, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, the monk directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision <note>original: "ñāṇa-dassana"</note>. He understands this: "This is my body, possessed of form, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished by rice and porridge, subject to impermanence, to being worn away, rubbed away, broken, and dispersed. And this is my <term>viññāṇa</term> <gloss>consciousness</gloss>, which is fixed here and bound up here."

70. Just as if, Great King, there were a beautiful beryl gem, naturally pure, eight-faceted, well-polished, clear, bright, limpid, and possessing all good qualities; and through it was strung a thread—blue, yellow, red, white, or light brown. A man with good sight, taking it in his hand, would reflect: "This is a beautiful beryl gem, naturally pure, eight-faceted, well-polished, clear, bright, limpid, and possessing all good qualities. Here is the thread strung through it—blue, yellow, red, white, or light brown."

<summary>This page describes the attainment of the fourth meditative absorption and the subsequent development of insight into the relationship between the physical body and consciousness. The Buddha uses the similes of a man wrapped in white cloth and a beryl gem on a string to illustrate these states of clarity.</summary>
